title: PLATE-VS: a web server for protein-ligand assay curation and cross-target virtual screening datasets.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Called the drugbench.org API (no login needed). The molecules endpoint reports 2,390,046 rows in total. A bulk POST download is capped at 200,000 rows per request. I downloaded all Ki records (67,878 rows, not truncated) and 200,000 IC50 records (truncated): 682 UniProt targets, 192,307 molecules, 6,733 source documents. Every row is in nM with a pChEMBL value (the negative log of molar affinity; 2 nulls). SMILES are present. 31,092 of 225,017 protein-molecule pairs have repeat measurements, with a median within-pair SD (standard deviation) of 0.17 log units. The 5-HT2A target (P28223) has 1,162 actives and 4,590 decoys, which are tagged standard_type=DECOY, activity_comment=deepcoy_decoy. The protein-cluster split CSV (qcov 70, threshold 0.7) has 837 UniProt IDs in 286 clusters; the largest cluster holds 202 of them. The SDF archive (ligand structure files) for threshold 0.7 is 312 MB on S3 (cloud storage); size only, not downloaded.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The count of 333,748 active records over 837 targets. The cross-assay Pearson correlations (0.80 and 0.878). The per-ligand train/test labels: I did not find these in the activity CSV, and they are presumably in the SDF archives. The hard/soft split definitions and the enrichment-factor results on the 15-target test set. The decoy-generation settings.

a1_downloadable.note: Checked in files: the open API and CSV downloads work without login. Each request returns at most 200,000 rows, so the full set must be pulled in chunks, filtered by target or by assay type.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Checked in files: pchembl_value (negative log molar affinity) and standard_value in nM are columns. The active-versus-decoy label is also a column (standard_type=DECOY). The protein-cluster split is a ready CSV.

a3_inputs_present.note: Checked in files: canonical SMILES (text strings describing each molecule) are on every row. Proteins come only as UniProt accessions, so 837 sequences must be fetched from UniProt: a trivial batch lookup.

a4_units_stated.note: Checked in files: the standard_units column reads nM for all 267,878 active rows I downloaded.

a5_enough_rows.note: Rows I actually downloaded (all Ki plus a truncated IC50 pull). The paper says 333,748 actives in total, plus about 1.97M decoys.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~50 MB actives CSV; ~300 MB with decoys
a6_fits_laptop.note: Estimated from the 29.6 MB size of a 200,000-row download. Fingerprints plus frozen embeddings run fine on a CPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Checked against the API: it reports 2,390,046 total entries; the paper says 2,390,001, a 45-row difference. The split CSV lists exactly 837 targets, matching the paper. I did not count the full active total of 333,748.

a8_label_provenance.note: Affinities are measured Ki/IC50 values from ChEMBL, a public bioactivity database. The negatives, however, are decoys generated by DeepCoy, a deep-learning decoy generator, not measured inactives. Any active-versus-decoy task therefore partly measures how well a model spots generated molecules.

B1.why: Activity rows and the protein-cluster CSV join cleanly on UniProt ID; ligand split labels sit in separate SDF archives.

B2.why: The CSVs parsed with pandas on the first try; only a mixed-type warning on activity_comment.

B3.why: In files: pChEMBL is precomputed, but Ki and IC50 are mixed and not directly comparable without a policy.

B4.why: In files: no relation or qualifier column, all values exact nM; the paper says only exact values were kept.

B5.why: In files: 31,092 pairs have repeat measurements with a median SD of 0.17 log; easy to average.

B6.why: Columns are ChEMBL field names and self-explanatory, but I found no data dictionary on the site or in the client.

C1.why: Accuracy decay versus pocket similarity is informative, but the authors and a 2026 arXiv paper already ran it.

C2.why: Open models (GEMS, DeepDTA, GraphDTA, the authors' own ESM-2 baselines) already evaluated on protein-cluster splits.

C3.why: Weak angle: only re-benchmarking frozen protein and ligand embeddings on an already-honest split.

C4.why: Affinity assays are costly, but docking (GNINA) already beats ligand-only ML on the hard split.

C5.why: Published per-target enrichment factors and baseline code in the Zenodo archive (paper and Zenodo metadata).

D1.why: ESM-2 (proteins) and ChemBERTa/MolFormer (molecules) have open weights.

D2.why: 837 protein embeddings plus about 240k ligand embeddings can be cached once on a CPU.

D3.why: Code is MIT-licensed (Zenodo); the underlying ChEMBL data is CC BY-SA.

E1.why: In files: protein-cluster split CSVs at 4 coverage levels by 6 thresholds.

E2.why: In files: 286 clusters at qcov70/threshold 0.7, though one cluster holds 202 of 837 targets.

E3.why: Per-target mean pChEMBL and random enrichment are trivial dummies.

E4.why: In files: 31,092 repeat pairs, median SD 0.17; the paper reports a cross-assay correlation of 0.80.

E5.why: The soft-versus-hard split gap should reappear, and molecular weight from SMILES is a trivial target.

E6.why: Label shuffling and protein-embedding ablation are straightforward.

E7.why: PDBbind CleanSplit is used by the authors; BindingDB is an independent affinity source.

E8.why: Paper reports enrichment factors on a 15-target test set, with code on Zenodo; ligand split labels unverified.

G1.why: In files: UniProt, ChEMBL molecule/target/assay/document IDs and SMILES.

G2.why: BindingDB and full ChEMBL, joinable on UniProt plus InChIKey or SMILES; AlphaFold DB on UniProt.

G3.why: Many measurements per pair; collapse by median pChEMBL per protein-molecule pair.

G4.why: A join adds more data but answers no new question beyond what PLATE-VS already frames.

H1.why: In files: negatives are DeepCoy-generated decoys; measured inactives (censored values) were removed.

H2.why: In files: 6,733 source documents and 682+ human-centric targets.

H3.why: Claim is stated precisely in honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Paper is explicit that decoys are generated and that only targets with a crystal structure are included.

I1.why: Katritch lab (USC) and the virtual-screening benchmarking community.

I2.why: Could shift choice between ligand-ML and docking, but the paper already shows docking wins.

I3.why: Bayes enrichment factor at 1% matches the screening decision of which compounds to test.

I4.why: Cross-target affinity is genuinely complex; per-target means fail on unseen clusters.

J1.why: Real modelling: grouped splits, frozen embeddings, transfer across protein clusters.

J2.why: Medicinal-chemistry plausibility is checkable with some effort.

J3.why: A clean decay curve of accuracy versus pocket similarity is shareable at any stage.

existing_models.name: PLATE-VS authors' baselines (RF/GBM/SVM on ECFP4 fingerprints, +ESM-2 embeddings, a graph neural network with cross-attention, GNINA and UniDock2 docking)
existing_models.score_and_split: Per-target Bayes enrichment factor at 1% on a 15-target hard split (unseen protein clusters): docking best, ligand-only ML near random; exact values were not rendered in the retrieved text.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Ligand-only ML collapses on unseen protein clusters; frozen ESM-2 recovers only part of the lost signal.

existing_models.name: GEMS (graph neural network with protein language-model embeddings, trained on PDBbind CleanSplit)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported state-of-the-art on the CASF benchmark after removing train-test leakage (exact numbers not retrieved).

existing_models.name: Beyond Random Splits (arXiv 2610.03456): 12 ESM-2-based drug-target affinity architectures
existing_models.score_and_split: 718,800 ChEMBL/BindingDB pairs; RMSE (root mean squared error) rises from 0.95 under scaffold splits to 1.30 under protein-cluster splits.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Model rankings reorganise under protein and dual out-of-distribution shifts.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model, 150M or 650M checkpoint) plus ChemBERTa or MolFormer (molecule language models)
backbone.licence: MIT (ESM-2); ChemBERTa and MolFormer are open

integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a model trained on ChEMBL-derived PLATE-VS clusters keep its accuracy on BindingDB measurements for proteins from unseen pocket clusters?

controls.positive_control: Recover the soft-versus-hard split gap reported in the paper; predict molecular weight from SMILES near-perfectly.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle pChEMBL within training targets; ablate the ESM-2 block, which should leave hard-split accuracy unchanged if protein features carry no transferable signal.
controls.external_validation: PDBbind CleanSplit (used by the authors) or BindingDB records not in ChEMBL.

honest_claim_h3: Predicts ChEMBL Ki/IC50 affinity, or separates actives from DeepCoy-generated decoys, for human-centric drug targets that have a co-crystal structure, when the test proteins come from pocket clusters unseen in training.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein's sequence and a small molecule's structure to predict how tightly the molecule binds proteins unlike any seen in training.
plain_idea.train_on: Protein-molecule pairs: the protein sequence and the molecule's text structure string (SMILES). I verified 267,878 measured pairs; the paper reports 333,748 in total.
plain_idea.predict: Binding strength as pChEMBL (negative log of the Ki or IC50 concentration), measured in lab assays and collected from published papers by ChEMBL.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Virtual-screening groups would learn whether cheap sequence-based models can stand in for docking on new protein families; the paper already suggests they mostly cannot.

label_elsewhere.sources: ChEMBL and BindingDB (known resources; PLATE-VS itself is a filtered subset of ChEMBL).
label_elsewhere.join_key: UniProt accession + InChIKey or ChEMBL compound ID
label_elsewhere.why: Millions of further affinity measurements allow external tests on proteins outside the 837 PLATE-VS targets.

pitch.headline: A free open API returns 268k nM-unit affinity rows over 682 targets, with protein-cluster splits ready-made for 837 targets.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Measured affinities, generated decoys (about 4 per active for 5-HT2A, a serotonin receptor), and pocket-similarity clusters in one source; 31,092 repeated pairs give a noise floor of 0.17 log units.
pitch.the_win: A frozen ESM-2 plus ChemBERTa head that lifts hard-split enrichment at 1% clearly above the paper's ESM-2 random-forest baseline on its 15 test targets.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A curve of accuracy versus pocket-similarity threshold across 24 split settings, which partly duplicates work the authors already did.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Katritch lab and virtual-screening benchmark users who are choosing between ligand-based ML and docking for new targets.

ml_idea: Train frozen ESM-2 protein embeddings plus molecule embeddings (or fingerprints) with a gradient-boosting or MLP (small neural network) head to predict pChEMBL. Evaluate on PLATE-VS protein-cluster splits across all 6 thresholds by 4 coverage levels, plotting accuracy against pocket similarity. Add a BindingDB external test.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed. 837 ESM-2 sequences take minutes; about 240k ChemBERTa ligand embeddings take roughly 2 h on CPU; LightGBM on 300k rows takes minutes per fold.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Find where the per-ligand train/test labels live (the 312 MB SDF archives?), and check whether the hard split leaves at least 15 test targets with at least 50 actives each.

verdict_reason: The data is clean, open and passes Part A in the files. But cross-target affinity prediction is crowded: the authors already benchmarked ESM-2 plus fingerprint baselines and docking on these exact splits, and open models such as GEMS exist. C2 = 0 and C-total = 5, so there is no clear angle.
